lessons.title: ಇರು (iru) — "to be, to stay, to live"
lessons.gloss: to be, to stay, to live

segments.text: You have already used this verb — in "how are you." Now meet it in its own right, and use it to say where you live.
ಇ (independent i) + ರು (ru) becomes ಇರು (iru).

ಇರು (iru, "to be, to exist, to stay, to live") is native Dravidian — the very same iru Tamil uses, and the verb behind Chapter 3's hēgiddīrā ("how are you") and cennāgiddēne ("I'm well"). It also means "to reside": ನಾನು ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಇದ್ದೇನೆ (nānu Beṅgaḷūrinalli iddēne, "I live in Bangalore"). One verb covers "be," "stay," and "live."

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: "in" comes after the noun

segments.text: ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನಲ್ಲಿ (Beṅgaḷūrinalli) = Bengaḷūru + -ಅಲ್ಲಿ (-alli, "in"), glued to the end of the noun. Kannada uses postpositions (case-suffixes) where English uses prepositions: "Bangalore-in I am," the verb last.

segments.text: The last verb of the chapter — and, like Hindi's karnā and Tamil's sey, it is a "do" verb that builds a hundred others.
ಕೆಲಸ (kelasa, "work"): ಕೆ (ke) + ಲ (la) + ಸ (sa). ಮಾಡು (māḍu, "do"): ಮಾ (mā) + ಡು (ḍu).
ಮಾಡು (māḍu, "to do, to make") is a core native Dravidian verb, and Kannada — like Hindi with karnā, Tamil with sey, and Telugu with cēyu — builds compound verbs by putting a noun in front of it:
ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡು (kelasa māḍu) = "work-do" = "to work" (kelasa, "work").
ಅಡುಗೆ ಮಾಡು (aḍuge māḍu) = "to cook".
ಸಹಾಯ ಮಾಡು (sahāya māḍu) = "to help" (sahāya from Sanskrit).
So "I work" is ನಾನು ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡುತ್ತೇನೆ (nānu kelasa māḍuttēne). Notice sahāya māḍu ("to help") pairs a Sanskrit noun with the native māḍu — Kannada's two vocabularies working together in one verb.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: noun + ಮಾಡು = a new verb

segments.text: This "noun + māḍu" pattern is the exact twin of Hindi's "noun + karnā," Tamil's "noun + sey," and Telugu's "noun + cēyu." Four languages — two of them from an unrelated family — all landed on the same trick.

segments.instruction: the Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu twins of this trick (karnā, sey, cēyu)

segments.text: How does Kannada turn "work" into "to work," and what verbs work the same way in its neighbours? (Kelasa + māḍu = "work-do"; Hindi karnā, Tamil sey, Telugu cēyu.)

segments.text: So far, "to be." Here is a verb that does something — and it shows how Kannada builds "I do X."
ಮಾ (mā) + ತ (ta) + ನಾ (nā) + ಡು (ḍu) becomes ಮಾತನಾಡು (mātanāḍu).

ಮಾತನಾಡು (mātanāḍu, "to speak, to talk") is native Dravidian, built on ಮಾತು (mātu, "word, speech") + āḍu ("to play/do") — "to word-play," i.e. to converse. To say "I speak," Kannada adds a two-part ending to the stem:
mātanāḍ- + -utt- (present) + -ēne ("I") becomes ಮಾತನಾಡುತ್ತೇನೆ (mātanāḍuttēne), "I speak."
The -ಏನೆ (-ēne) ending is "I," so nānu is rarely needed. Change the ending, change the person: mātanāḍuttāne (he), mātanāḍuttāḷe (she), mātanāḍuttāre (they / you-respectful).

Every Kannada verb is built this way — a stem, a tense-marker, a person-ending. And, like Tamil and Telugu, Kannada marks no gender in the first person: mātanāḍuttēne is the same for a man or a woman.
Build "I speak" from mātanāḍu, and name the noun it's built on. (Mātanāḍuttēne; mātu, "word / speech.")

segments.text: Your first full, moving sentence — and it names one of the classical languages of India.
ಕನ್ನಡ (kannaḍa): ಕ (ka) + ನ್ನ (nna, doubled) + ಡ (ḍa).

ನಾನು ಕನ್ನಡ ಮಾತನಾಡುತ್ತೇನೆ = ನಾನು (nānu, "I") + ಕನ್ನಡ (kannaḍa, the object) + ಮಾತನಾಡುತ್ತೇನೆ (mātanāḍuttēne, "speak") — "I Kannada speak," the verb last as always. The name ಕನ್ನಡ (kannaḍa) is native (often linked to kar-nāḍu, "the black/high land," whence Karnataka). Kannada has a literature over a thousand years old and holds the second-most Jnanpith literary awards of any Indian language — a classical tongue, spoken by some fifty million.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: no gender on "I speak"

segments.text: Mātanāḍuttēne is the same whether a man or a woman says it — Kannada, like Tamil and Telugu, marks no gender in the first or second person (only the third: -āne he, -āḷe she). This is unlike Hindi, where even "I speak" changes for the speaker's gender (boltā/boltī).
